phonemes.desc: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ], like English 'shoe' — the sound of rushing air.
Long close back vowel, sustained like a drawn-out breath; the name itself resembles an exhalation.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SHOO' — drawn out, breathy, like the sound of wind passing through a corridor.

kin.label: Egyptian

kin.form: ϣⲟⲩ (šou), 'air, wind' — the late reflex of the word (Allen 2013)

pronunciation.note: Shu is Tier 1 because the Egyptian Šw preserves the caron-marked š — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. The name is an onomatopoeic masterpiece: šw sounds like the rush of air it names. Egyptologists debate whether the primary meaning is 'dryness', 'emptiness', or 'he who rises up'; the god contains all three.

domains.title: The Breath Between Worlds
domains.subtitle: Air · Wind · Lions
domains.lead: Šw is the air that separates earth from sky, the breath that brings consciousness, the light that makes visibility possible. In Heliopolitan theology he is the first being to emerge from the creator Atum — not by procreation alone, but by breath, spittle, or sneeze. His eternal labour is to hold the sky-goddess Nut above the earth-god Geb, so that the space of life can exist between them.

cards.name: Air and Breath
cards.desc: Shu is the atmosphere itself — invisible, life-giving, and inseparable from consciousness.

cards.name: Cosmic Separation
cards.desc: With arms raised, Shu lifts Nut away from Geb, creating the interval in which all life dwells.

cards.name: Light
cards.desc: The rays of the sun are called the 'Shu-forms of Re'; Shu makes seeing possible by making space luminous.

cards.name: The Lion
cards.desc: Shu sometimes takes leonine form as a fighter and defender, paired with Tefnut's lioness form.

symbols.name: Ostrich feather
symbols.meaning: Lightness, air, and truth; Shu wears one or more feathers on his head

symbols.name: Raised arms
symbols.meaning: The posture of Shu supporting the sky; the hieroglyph for ka-arms also echoes his life-giving embrace

symbols.name: Lion
symbols.meaning: Shu's fighting aspect; the dry, parching wind of the desert

symbols.name: Ankh
symbols.meaning: The breath of life that Shu carries into every nostril

symbols.name: Four supports / Ogdoad
symbols.meaning: The eight Heh-gods who assist Shu in holding up the heavens

mythology.lead: Shu's mythology is cosmogony in motion. He is not a hero who goes on quests; he is the first differentiation of the creator, the void that becomes space, the breath that makes the world inhabitable. Without him, Nut and Geb would remain locked together and no life could arise.

myths.title: Born from Atum
myths.text: In the oldest Egyptian creation account we possess — Pyramid Text Utterance 600, inscribed in the royal pyramids of the late Old Kingdom — the creator Atum stands alone on the primeval hill in the waters of Nun and, without companion, brings forth the first two gods: he sneezes Shu and spits Tefnut, the sacred text says, and the wordplay is the theology. Shu's very name (šw) echoes the sneeze, Tefnut's the spittle; the world begins with the creator's own body discharging itself into differentiation. The Coffin Texts (spells 75–80) expand the scene: Atum, alone in Nun, says he was not built by any builder, and then — 'I sneezed Shu, I spat Tefnut'. Whether by sneeze, spittle, or exhalation, Shu is the moment creation becomes conscious: the first breath the universe ever takes. The myth's joke is profound — the cosmos as a sneeze — and its claim deeper: life begins not with matter but with air, the lightest thing that exists, without which no god, king, or field can live.

myths.title: Shu Lifts the Sky
myths.text: Shu and Tefnut beget the twins Geb (earth) and Nut (sky), but the children are locked in an embrace that leaves no room for life. Shu places himself in the interval and raises Nut above his head, arching her body into the starry vault — the posture the Egyptians gave him forever: kneeling or standing, arms lifted, the cosmic pillar. The image saturates Egyptian religion. It fills royal tombs from the Book of the Dead papyrus of the scribe Nakht (TT52) to the burial chamber of Horemheb (KV57); the Late Period Book of Nut diagrams it as an astronomical treatise; and every temple doorway flanked by heh-pillars and every palace façade propped by figures with raised arms is a frozen Shu. The Ennead of Heliopolis is thus not only a genealogy but a physics: Atum's first act of self-differentiation, perpetually maintained by his firstborn son. Order is not a state but a held pose — and the sky stays up only because someone never puts his arms down.

myths.title: Shu and Tefnut in Nubia
myths.text: A late myth tells how Tefnut quarrelled with Shu and departed south to Nubia, taking the form of a lioness — or, in the Demotic telling, of a cat travelling with her companion baboon. The land dried behind her; the south wind brought no relief. Shu sent Thoth, master of words, disguised as a baboon, to talk her home; his flood of eloquence — stories, flattery, argument, and embedded animal fables — accomplished what force could not. The Demotic Myth of the Sun's Eye (Papyrus Leiden I 384) and the Ptolemaic Papyrus Jumilhac preserve the journey, and the returning eye is welcomed in festival. The myth explains the dry wind from the south and the coming of moisture, but its deeper subject is the first marriage: Shu is air, Tefnut moisture, and dry air alone is desolation. It also quietly honors its own medium — the world is saved by eloquence, not arms. In Egypt's most literate civilization, even the weather is talked home.

myths.title: Shu in the Afterlife
myths.text: Funerary texts make Shu the atmosphere of salvation. The dead are promised they will not thirst because of Shu and will not hunger because of Tefnut; the ascension utterances of the Pyramid Texts give the king a ladder and a wind, and the Coffin Texts teach that to become an akh — an effective, transfigured spirit — is to breathe Shu again. In the Book of the Dead the justified sail the sky in Re's barque through the very air Shu is, and spell 15 greets the solar retinue in which he stands at the prow of the night voyage. Breath is the thread on which Egyptian immortality is strung: the heart must be light, the name must live, and the lungs must fill — in the Duat as in Memphis. The afterlife was not imagined as ghostly ether but as weather: a climate maintained by the same god who first separated sky from ground. To die was to change skies, not to stop breathing.

myths.title: Shu on the Throne
myths.text: Egypt's king-lists did not begin with men. The Turin Royal Canon, compiled in the Ramesside age, records the gods themselves as Egypt's first rulers — Re, then Shu, then Geb, Osiris, Seth, Horus — reigning for tens of thousands of years before the human dynasties begin. Shu thus appears not only as a cosmological principle but as a precedent for pharaonic office: the god of air once wore the crown and governed the Two Lands. The tradition explains the throne's succession as the Ennead's own — power descending from creator to breath to earth to the murdered and avenged Osiris — giving every later king a genealogy that was also a cosmology. No narrative survives of what Shu did in his reign; the canon gives years, not deeds, and the entry alone testifies. But its placement is the point: between the creator and the earth stands the god of the interval, and kingship, like air, is what fills the space between heaven and ground.

lore.syncretism: The Greeks associated Shu with Atlas, the Titan who holds up the celestial sphere — a comparison of function, not of name, since no Greek rendering of šw is attested; modern scholars repeat the comparison on the same grounds. In Egyptian theology Shu could merge with Re (as the rays of sunlight) and with Onuris, the warrior god. Later solar theology made Shu the son of Re as well as of Atum, smoothing local variants into a single cosmic scheme. The image of a figure supporting the heavens passed from Egypt into Hellenistic and medieval cosmography, influencing depictions of the celestial spheres.
lore.culturalLegacy: Shu survives wherever we say 'atmosphere' and mean more than weather. The Greeks, meeting the image of a figure bearing heaven, supplied the parallel of Atlas — a comparison every Egyptology handbook repeats — and the sky-bearer motif migrated through Hellenistic and medieval art into the atlantes of Renaissance architecture, carved men holding up what cannot be held. Modern science gave his domain a name and a fragility: the atmosphere is now known to be thin, held, and breakable — Shu's arms, imaged by satellites. Breath-work, meditation, and singing traditions treat every inhalation as a microcosm of his labour: to breathe is to separate inside from outside and to hold, for a moment, the space in which life happens. Few gods have aged so well into metaphor without losing their physics.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Shu is the god of the interval. He is what happens between earth and sky, between inhalation and exhalation, between the word and its meaning. We rarely notice him because he is what we move through; he is the invisible precondition of every visible thing. To become conscious of Shu is to realise that emptiness is not nothing. The space between bodies, between stars, between sounds — these intervals are as real as the things they separate.

In an age of clutter and noise, Shu asks us to respect the void. The sky is not a blue screen but a held breath. The silence between notes is not absence but architecture. The pause before speaking is where intention gathers. Shu teaches that separation is a form of love: by holding Nut away from Geb, he creates the room in which all living things can breathe. To name him Šw is to hear, in two letters, the rush of that creating distance.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name šw is written with the folded cloth (S29, phonogram š) and the quail-chick (G43, phonogram w), often with the air/light determinatives. The letter š represents a voiceless postalveolar fricative, like English 'sh'. In older transliteration systems the same sound is written ś or sh; the PUNICODEX form follows Gardiner and the Wörterbuch. The long vowel is inferred from Coptic ϣⲟⲩ and from the word's onomatopoeic quality.

lore.archaeology: Shu raising Nut above Geb is painted in the burial chamber of Horemheb (KV57) and on the Book of the Dead papyrus of the scribe Nakht (TT52, Metropolitan Museum). His ostrich feathers crown bronze and stone statuettes from the New Kingdom onward, and the 'Shu-pose' of raised arms develops into the heh-pillars that flank temple doorways. Reliefs at Karnak and in the Osireion at Abydos show him within the Heliopolitan ennead, and faience and stone feathers from his headgear appear among funerary amulets. The motif crosses media with ease — painted, carved, cast — because it is Egyptian cosmology's most portable sentence: someone holds up the sky.
